E1136.summary: An expression Atwood uses once, for the purpose towards which conviction is steeled. The text does not define it further.
E1136.body: Atwood speaks of “conviction steeled to the purpose of her Motive Light” [IV.4 ¶19]. The record gives no further definition.

E1137.summary: Atwood's term for man's life, set against man seen as the individualized multiplication of a blind will.
E1137.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “tat Motive Reason which is his life” [II.1 ¶42], so she identifies Motive Reason with man's life. She sets it against man as the individualized multiplication of a blind will [II.1 ¶42].

E1138.summary: A Latin motto cited in support of the First Matter as the one substance God created in the beginning.
E1138.body: The motto is cited (QUOTED) in support of the First Matter as the single substance God created: “Deus, cum solus fuisset in principio, Creavit unam substantiam, Hanc primam materiam nominamus.” [III.2 ¶56]. Our translation, which the book does not give: God, when he was alone in the beginning, created one substance; this we name the first matter. The same sentence also stands as the epigraph credited to Mylius [III.2 ¶2].

E1139.summary: Flammel's seven-fold mountain, with a royal herb at its top. Atwood equates it with several other symbols: Esdras's outgoings of paradise, Sendivogius's Planetary Sphere and the Sapphiric Mine's tincture.
E1139.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) describes Flammel's seven-fold mountain, at whose top a royal herb is found [II.4 ¶9]. She then equates it with other names: “Those seven mystic mountains, whereupon grow the roses and lilies, are the outgoings of paradise mentioned in Esdras” [II.4 ¶9]. She adds “and the Planetary Sphere of Sendivogius” and “and that most famous tincture of the Sapphiric Mine” [II.4 ¶9]. So the text treats these as several names for one thing. It does not state the plain meaning.

E1140.summary: In Proclus and the Phaedrus passage, the second grade of vision. It is seeing stable appearances with closed eye, through the pure soul, and comes through silence imparted by faith.
E1140.body: This term comes from quoted voices, not from Atwood. In the passage from Socrates in the Phaedrus (n15 cites Proclus), muesis is the second grade: “But we view with closed eye, i.e., with the pure soul itself (muoumetha) entire and stable appearances” [II.4 ¶23]. These appearances come through the connective gods [II.4 ¶23]. Proclus (QUOTED) says that “muesis, in short, is neither through intelligence nor judgment, but through the uncial silence imparted by faith” [II.4 ¶40], so faith is named as its cause. The text gives no further definition.

E1141.summary: Increasing the finished Stone or Medicine without limit by repeating the same operation: dissolving and coagulating it with its own mercury. Atwood also uses it of frauds' promises and of Light's assimilative virtue.
E1141.body:
Most records come from quoted authorities. Several describe it as the stage after the Stone is made, when its virtue is increased.

- Norton speaks of the Red Stone: “Him to increase in multiplication” [I.1 ¶60].
- Paracelsus says the tincture stays “immutable in the multiplication” [I.1 ¶76].
- *The Hunting of the Greene Lyon* says the Medicine is increased without restarting the work, best by continual fermentation: “It’s so well Multeplied as with continuall Firmentation:” [III.1 ¶65].
- The fraternity of the Rosy Cross makes it the fourth gate, together with augmentation: “The fourth gate is that of multiplication and augmentation in which proportions and weights are necessary.” Reaching this gate gives a universal medicine [III.3 ¶63].
- Eudoxus makes it the Sixth Key, “the Multiplication of the Stone, by the reiteration of the same operation”, which raises its virtues without limit [IV.3 ¶16].
- The Author of the Open Entrance writes: “It remains only for the work of Multiplication” [IV.3 ¶18]. He describes joining the Stone with Mercury of the First Work, then dissolving and coagulating it with its own mercury. Each round multiplies its virtue and goes faster [IV.3 ¶18].

A footnote of unclear voice describes the same repeated dissolution and coagulation by the water of the medicine's mercury, which raises its tinging virtue. It also says that “the multiplication of its internal form has rubified it” [I.3 n67].

Atwood herself (ATWOOD) uses the word in two other ways. First, frauds cheated merchants out of gold, silver and gems, “which they lost, in vain hope of getting them multiplied” [I.1 ¶55]. Second, she makes multiplying a property of Light alone: “Or what else should possibly transmute or multiply by its own assimilative virtue?” [IV.3 ¶30].

E1142.summary: The purely mineral goal to which many gave up their lives. Atwood contrasts it with the art's higher purposes.
E1142.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) describes those “sacrificing their whole life’s hope to the multiplication of gold” [I.1 ¶42]. She treats it as a merely mineral aim, set against the higher purposes of the art.

E1143.summary: The universal Spirit as it is first consciously revealed in humanity's receptive life. It can receive anything and be converted to anything, and it is equated with Aristotle's passive intellect.
E1143.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “the universal Mundane Spirit, as it is at first consciously revealed in the recipient life of humanity” [II.2 ¶17]. She says it can receive anything and be converted to anything. She equates it with what Aristotle names: “which Aristotle, in his Metaphysics, calls passive intellect” [II.2 ¶17].

E1144.summary: Purified or cleansed. The Spirit's mundification must be completed “in both kinds” before the Philosophic Work truly begins.
E1144.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) speaks of “the Phantastic Spirit before it is mundified” [II.2 ¶15]. In context the word apparently means purified. She also says the Philosophic Work does not truly begin “until the mundification of the Spirit is completed in both kinds” [IV.1 ¶48]. The text does not say what the two kinds are.

E1145.summary: The person addressed in an Orphic fragment as “offspring of the bright Silene”.
E1145.body: Musaeus appears only as the addressee of the Orphic fragment cited at [II.4 ¶40], where he is called the offspring of the bright Silene.

E1146.summary: A term used once for what appeared during the evaporative process of purification. What exactly it refers to is unclear.
E1146.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) writes: “And that such actually appeared to be the Musai, during the evaporative process of purification” [II.3 ¶22]. This comes in connection with the material images seen during that purification. The text does not make clear whether the Musai are those images or something else.

E1147.summary: A collection Atwood cites as containing works by Philalethes and the Water Stone.
E1147.body: Atwood cites this collection as the place where works by Philalethes and the Water Stone are found [I.1 ¶73; I.1 n83].

E1148.summary: The Greeks' name for the aspirants, whom the Hierophant passed on to the immortal abode.
E1148.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) gives Mustai as the Greek name for the aspirants: “the aspirants, by the Greeks called Mustai” [II.3 ¶36]. The Hierophant passed them on to the immortal abode [II.3 ¶36].

E1149.summary: Norton's master, quoted inside Norton's verse as revealing the secret that the vessel is glass.
E1149.body: Inside Norton's verse, his “good Master” is quoted (QUOTED) as revealing that the vessel is glass: “Si Deus non dedisset nobis vas Nihil dedisset” [III.4 ¶31]. Our translation, which the book does not give: If God had not given us the vessel, he would have given nothing.

E1150.summary: Author cited for the epigraph saying that God created one substance, the first matter.
E1150.body: Mylius (QUOTED), *Phil. Reform.*, Pars. VI, Lib. 1, gives the epigraph: “Deus, cum solus fuisset in principio, creavit unam substantiam; hanc primam materiam nominamus.” [III.2 ¶2]. Our translation: God, when he was alone in the beginning, created one substance; this we name the first matter. Atwood uses it in support of the one First Matter. The same words are cited again as a motto at [III.2 ¶56].

E1151.summary: The initiates who, according to the expounders, were given narcotic liquors before the shows.
E1151.body: This is the expounders' view (QUOTED: the expounders), which Atwood reports. They say narcotic liquors were given “which were administered to the Mystae before the shows commence” [II.4 ¶56].

E1152.summary: The initiates whose inner experience, Atwood says, the Neo-Platonists did not make public.
E1152.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), Atwood (ATWOOD) says: “It was not their practice to declare the inner experience of the Mystae and Teleioi” [APP ¶122]. “Their” refers to the Neo-Platonists.

E1153.summary: A French treatise Atwood cites in support of the conjunction of Mars and Venus yielding solar sulphur, repeated cooking until rainbow colours appear, and the magnetic work.
E1153.body: Atwood cites *Mystere de la Croix*, chap. 13 (spelled 'Mystere de la Crois' in n10), in support of three points. The first is the conjunction of Mars and Venus, which yields a solar sulphur. The second is repeated cooking until rainbow colours appear. The third is that the work is magnetic: “Cet ouvrage s’appelle Aimantique” [III.3 ¶11; III.3 n4; III.3 ¶18; III.3 n10]. Our translation: This work is called Magnetic. She uses it as support for her own view.

E1154.summary: The ancient initiatory rites, Ethnic and Christian, held at Eleusis and in Eastern temples. Atwood treats them as real, scientific inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source, connected with Alchemy.
E1154.body:
Atwood (ATWOOD) treats the Mysteries as real and effective, not as ceremony. They were initiatory rites, “both Ethnic and Christian”, that kept a secret apart from ordinary worship: “There was undoubtedly a secret, hanging about these celebrations, both Ethnic and Christian” [II.2 ¶5]. Their object was Ontological Wisdom, and they really obtained it [II.2 ¶5].

She holds that “the Hermetic purifications and Mysteries, celebrated in the Eastern temples and by the priests at Eleusis, were real and efficacious” [II.2 ¶24]. Their stages ran in order: revealment of the Medial Life, Purificative Rites, then final initiations [II.2 ¶24]. They worked a vital change in those who sought wisdom and immortality, and “the conduct of the Mysteries was uniform and entirely scientific” [III.1 ¶9].

In them, apparitions come before divine illumination, “wherein the consciousness, becoming artificially wrapped by the Mysteries” is held in Hades [II.3 ¶29]. She reads the Rosicrucian letter as describing a passage of initiatory progress within them [II.3 ¶29]. A passage of unclear voice speaks of Intellect “descending into the bosom of the Mysteries” when it perceives the Formless Subject [III.2 ¶55].

Historically, “Necessity, at length, compelled an abandonment of the Mysteries” after the fall of Alexandria, along with the banning of Theurgic rites [I.1 ¶30]. Synesius “was careful, however, to protect the mysteries of his religion from vulgar abuse” [I.1 ¶27]. Yet “the Mysteries of Antiquity changed their form only to appear more resplendent when Christianity came to be the prevailing religion” [IV.2 ¶17]. In Christianity they took the form of effectual baptismal regeneration and the Eucharist [IV.2 ¶17].

Atwood asks that the Mysteries of Eleusis and the rest be understood “not as mere external ceremonials, pictured scenes of suffering and beatitudes, but as real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source” [IV.4 ¶5]. She connects them with Alchemy [IV.4 ¶5].

E1155.summary: The Mysteries cited as a voice. They call Isis Athena, and their mandate forbade telling the revelation to the profane.
E1155.body: Atwood cites the Mysteries twice. In them Isis is called Athena, which expresses the Spirit's self-motion and intelligence [III.1 ¶63]. Their mandate forbade passing the revelation on to the profane [III.2 ¶46].

E1156.summary: The mysteries and their wise hierophants, cited to show that the mind must leave all images behind to perceive Divinity.
E1156.body: Atwood cites the mysteries and the wise hierophants as an illustration. The Aspirant leaves the statues behind to behold the Adytum, and this shows the mind leaving all images; it is “the order in which Divinity is perceived” [III.2 ¶66].

forms: Mysteries celebrated at Eleusis and the rest
E1157.summary: The Eleusinian and other Mysteries, which Atwood reinterprets as real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source, connected with Alchemy.
E1157.body: Atwood reinterprets the Mysteries of Eleusis and the rest as real inductions of the Understanding Spirit to its Source, not as external ceremonies. She connects them with Alchemy [IV.4 ¶5]. See also Mysteries.

E1158.summary: An adept, cited from Khunrath's Amphiteatr. Sap. Etern., who defines the philosopher's stone as embodied Ruach Elohim. Atwood admits such definitions explain the unknown by the more unknown.
E1158.body: Atwood quotes him: “The philosopher’s stone, says the mysterious adeptest, is Ruach Elohim” [III.3 ¶50]. The note cites Khunrath, *Amphiteatr. Sap. Etern.*, Isag. in fig. [III.3 n35]. He calls the Stone embodied Ruach Elohim, names Salt as its principle and calls it Wisdom [III.3 ¶50]. Atwood uses him in support but admits that such definitions explain the unknown by the more unknown [III.3 ¶50].

E1159.summary: The object of Agrippa's search. The Rosy Cross fraternity calls it the most ancient knowledge, breathed into nature by God's Word, and equates it with the Fire of Life and the Wise men's red gold.
E1159.body:
Atwood (ATWOOD) says Agrippa reached his final conviction by “searching and proving the magnitude of the Mystery” [I.1 ¶64].

The fraternity of the Rosy Cross (QUOTED) describes the mystery as the most ancient knowledge, “a knowledge which God Almighty, by his Word, breathed into nature” [III.3 ¶63]. It is given to few, though it lives and moves daily in sight of all [III.3 ¶63]. They equate it with “a miraculous power, the blessed Fire of Life” and with “the transparent carbuncle and red gold of the Wise men” [III.3 ¶63].

E1160.summary: The regenerative mystery, of which, Atwood says, the Reformers kept little more than a traditional faith.
E1160.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) says the Reformers kept little of it, “retaining, indeed, little more of the mystery of regeneration than a traditional faith” [I.1 ¶26].

E1161.summary: The one analysis that resolves a pot into gold and gold into an indissoluble water. It agrees with hermetic doctrine in both inner and outer senses, and its final stage yields Light.
E1161.body: Atwood (ATWOOD) writes: “For by no other analysis either is a pot resolved into gold, or gold into a water which is indissoluble.” [III.2 n38]. She holds that this analysis agrees with hermetic doctrine in both its internal and external senses, and that its ultimate stage yields Light [III.2 n38].

E1162.summary: A topic Atwood deliberately leaves aside at this point. She says it will be better understood once the Philosophic Subject is made manifest.
E1162.body: Atwood (ATWOOD): “We omit many things here relating to the mystical death and regeneration” [II.3 ¶56]. She says these will be better understood once the Philosophic Subject has been made manifest.

forms: the mystical problem of the Trinity
E1163.summary: The Trinity's “three in one and one in three”, cited as an analogy for agent, patient and offspring in all created things.
E1163.body: A footnote uses the mystical problem of the Trinity, “three in one and one in three”, as an analogy for the agent, patient and offspring found in all created things [I.3 n30]. The voice is not specified.

E1164.summary: Cited in the Appendix as foreshadowing the mystery of “two Causes and one Mother”.
E1164.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the myth of Oedipus is said to foreshadow the mystery of “two Causes and one Mother” [APP ¶73].

E1165.summary: The Myths, cited in the Appendix for showing Vulcan as lame. This is explained as halting motion.
E1165.body: In the Appendix (Table Talk, a later layer), the Myths are cited for showing Vulcan as lame, which is explained as halting motion [APP ¶129].
